title: The Checkout Drop-Off
summary: Cartly is a checkout optimization platform for small e-commerce stores — it helps merchants recover abandoned carts and convert hesitant buyers. Its customers are store owners who pay monthly per active store.

Q1.text: Checkout abandonment has jumped from 62% to 78% over the last month. What do you do first?

choices.text: Break down abandonment by step in the checkout flow
choices.reveal: Most drop-off now happens at the payment method screen — up from 15% to 45% of all abandonments.
choices.because: Breaking the funnel into steps isolates where the move happened — the jump is concentrated, not uniform.

choices.text: Interview three customers who abandoned in the last week
choices.reveal: Two cited a confusing new payment options screen; one had a technical error. Pattern is forming but sample is thin.

choices.text: Check whether a recent deployment changed the checkout page
choices.reveal: No deployment touched checkout in the last month — the change is behavioral, not technical.

choices.text: Launch an abandoned-cart email re-engagement campaign
choices.reveal: The emails go out — but they re-engage the same 18% recovery rate. The drop-off source is untouched.

Q2.text: Payment method screen is now where 45% of abandonments happen, up from 15%. What do you investigate next?

choices.text: Compare the payment screen before and after the last UI refresh
choices.reveal: The refresh added a scrolling list of 11 payment icons. Users pause scrolling before choosing.
choices.because: The UI change is dated and the new element is exactly where the drop concentrated.

choices.text: Segment abandonment by device type
choices.reveal: Mobile shows slightly higher abandonment, but desktop jumped too — the issue is not device-specific.

choices.text: Survey users who reached the payment screen but didn't complete
choices.reveal: Surveys mention 'too many options' but the sample is thin.

choices.text: A/B test removing regional payment methods
choices.reveal: The test runs — but without a hypothesis about why the screen changed behavior, the result is hard to interpret.

Q3.text: Two of three interviewed customers mentioned a confusing payment options screen. What do you do next?

choices.text: Expand interviews to 10 more recent abandoners to confirm the pattern
choices.reveal: 6 of 10 new interviews mention the payment screen — pattern holds, 4 specifically name the scrolling icon list.
choices.because: More interviews confirm the pattern and isolate the specific element causing friction.

choices.text: Use the three interviews to scope a fix for the payment screen
choices.reveal: The fix is scoped — but without confirming across more users, the scope may solve the wrong problem.

choices.text: Drop the interviews and rely on the funnel breakdown instead
choices.reveal: The funnel already showed where the drop happened — but without the 'why', the fix may miss the root cause.

Q4.text: The payment screen shows 11 scrolling payment icons, and users pause before choosing. What do you do?

choices.text: Prioritize simplifying the payment screen to show the 3 most-used methods first
choices.reveal: Engineering estimates 3 days. The 3 most-used methods cover 82% of completed checkouts.
choices.because: The fix is small in scope and targets the exact screen where behavior changed — cost-benefit is clear.

choices.text: Run a full redesign of the checkout flow
choices.reveal: The redesign is scoped at 6 weeks and cuts 4 other features — for a payment-screen issue, the cost is disproportionate.

choices.text: Add a tooltip explaining each payment method
choices.reveal: Tooltips clarify methods — but users still pause to read them all before choosing.

Q5.text: Simplifying the payment screen to 3 methods is estimated at 3 days. How do you validate before full rollout?

choices.text: Roll out to 20% of stores and compare payment-screen completion against the prior week
choices.reveal: The 20% cohort's payment completion rises from 55% to 71% — a clear lift tied to the change.
choices.because: A staged rollout with before/after comparison isolates the change's effect from other variables.

choices.text: Ship to all stores and monitor overall abandonment next month
choices.reveal: Next month's abandonment drops — but without a comparison group, you can't tell if it was the payment change or a seasonal shift.

choices.text: Ask 3 interviewed customers to test the simplified screen
choices.reveal: The 3 customers say the screen is clearer — but this is qualitative, no measurement of actual conversion.

Q6.text: The simplified payment screen shows conversion up from 55% to 71%. What's your final validation step?

choices.text: A/B test the simplified screen against the original to confirm the lift holds
choices.reveal: The A/B test confirms: simplified screen at 71% vs original at 55%. The lift is real and stable.
choices.because: An A/B test against the original confirms the lift is from the change, not other factors.

choices.text: Monitor weekly conversion for the next month
choices.reveal: Weekly conversion holds at 71% — but without a control, you can't be certain it's not a seasonal pattern.

choices.text: Report success to the client and close the ticket
choices.reveal: The ticket is closed — but without a controlled validation, the success claim is incomplete.

Q7.text: You shipped to all stores and monthly abandonment dropped. But you can't isolate the cause. What do you do to understand the lift?

choices.text: Run a quick A/B test on 5% of traffic to isolate the payment screen's effect
choices.reveal: The A/B test on 5% shows the simplified screen converts 68% vs 54% for the control. The lift is from the payment screen change, not seasonality.
choices.because: A quick A/B test on a small sample isolates the payment screen's effect quickly without delaying the rollout.

choices.text: Attribute the drop to the payment screen change and move on
choices.reveal: The drop is attributed to the payment screen — but without validation, you can't be sure. Next month a regression could be missed.

choices.text: Run a full retrospective analysis of all changes in the last month
choices.reveal: The retrospective finds the payment screen change plus a seasonal discount period. The analysis can't separate the two effects.

Q8.text: The A/B test confirms the payment screen change drove a 14-point conversion lift. The client asks if there are more improvements. What do you investigate next?

choices.text: Review the next-highest drop-off step in the funnel for similar simplification opportunities
choices.reveal: The shipping address step has a 12% drop-off — field validation errors appear before submission. Simplifying the form layout could reduce that drop-off.
choices.because: The next-highest drop-off step with a clear friction point is the natural next target for optimization.

choices.text: Survey customers about what else they want improved
choices.reveal: Survey responses are mixed — some want faster checkout, some want more payment options, some want guest checkout. The signal is fragmented.

choices.text: Recommend a full checkout redesign to capture all friction points
choices.reveal: The full redesign is scoped at 8 weeks — but the payment screen fix just delivered, and the address step's friction is isolated and smaller in scope.

criteria.label: Letting evidence lead
criteria.guidance: Name the driver before betting the fix.

criteria.label: Sizing customer impact
criteria.guidance: Ground the decision in what changes for the buyer.

criteria.label: Proving the outcome
criteria.guidance: Define the measure that separates the fix's effect from noise.

criteria.label: Making the trade-off explicit
criteria.guidance: Name what each direction costs — scope, time, or roadmap space.
